The Alexandria National Museum is a true architectural gem, housed in a stunning Italian-style villa that serves as a beautiful backdrop for Egypt’s rich history. The collection is impressive, spanning from the Pharaonic era through the Graeco-Roman, Coptic, and Islamic periods. It offers a much more intimate and manageable experience than the larger museums in Cairo.
However, it is heartbreaking to see such a significant site lacking proper upkeep. The building and several exhibits clearly need more attention and maintenance; issues with lighting, dust, and aging displays detract from the overall experience. Furthermore, the visitor experience would be greatly improved if the staff were better trained and more professional. At times, the service feels indifferent, and there is a missed opportunity for guided insights that could bring these artifacts to life.
With a bit of investment in facility care and staff development, this museum could easily be a world-class destination. It’s worth a visit for the history alone, but it definitely needs a "refresh."

HIDDEN TREASURES OF ALEXANDRIA’S ANTIQUITIES MUSEUM

The Antiquities Museum is located directly in front of the main Alexandria Library (Alexandrina Bibliotheca). In fact, it forms an integrated part of the modern library complex. We visited this place for a brief time, after visiting the library complex on a Sundary noon in the month of January 2026. We were part of a big group to undertake the visit. This was opened to public in 2002 and presents a compact narrative of the city’s layered history. Interestingly, the number of people who visit this museum, compared to those who visit the library complex per se, are less in number.

We were told that there are over 1300 artefacts here, organised chronologically from Ancient Egypt period through Greek, Roman, Byzantine and early Islamic era.  There is considerable representation of the objects recovered from the Mediterranean sea near Alexandria through underwater excavations, reflecting the subterranean city’s ancient past.

Of the objects exhibited, the key ones include colossal statues of gods and ruler, sarcophagi, mummies, mosaics, coins, glassware, jewels and items of every day use. They give us a glimpse of the power of the kings and the life of ordinary mortals in this ancient city on the eastern side of the Mediterranean.
We find the design and organisation quite modern, with good signages and providing the visitors a good perspective of the history in a short time. It adds and complements the library, by combining its vision of knowledge with the material wealth of ancient city of Alexandria.

The museum is worth a quick 30 minutes visit, after taking a more detailed stroll in the library complex.

It was built by the Roman charioteer Ezadoras (Isidore) as a thank giving for Isis, on the recovery of his foot which was broken when he fell off his chariot.

The temple consists of a platform built of limestone and approached by a staircase. In the middle of the platform, there is a small pedestal on which the votive marble statue of Ezadoras was placed.
There are also four Ionic marble columns and five marble statues were placed between them;
The 1st statue:
It belongs to Hermanubis, who is depicted as a young man wearing a Greek tunic with a torch in his hand. Next to his feet, there is a seated figure of Jackal (Anubis).
The 2nd statue:
It belongs to god Harpocratis who is depicted as a naked child with his thumb in his mouth, he is also shown with a side-lock of hair.
The 3rd statue:
It is the largest one and it belongs to goddess Isis who is depicted in the Greek form as a standing figure of a woman wearing a tunic with a knot on her dress, she is also crowned with two horns and a sun disk, and she holds the situla (jar for sacred water).
The 4th and 5th statues:
They are for god Osiris in canopic form, he is represented as a jar and its lid takes the shape of the head of god Osiris.

The pedestal, the votive marble foot and 5 marble statues are right now in the Antiquities Museum of The New Library of Alexandria, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina.

I used to go there when I was young [long time ago 😄] People called it Ras el Soda temple - I got these informations from Google Bard The Greco-Roman temple of Ras el Soda is a small, well-preserved temple located in Alexandria, Egypt. It was discovered in 1936 and is the only private temple ever found in Alexandria. The temple was built in the 2nd century AD by a Roman charioteer named Isidorus as a thank-you to the goddess Isis for healing him from an injury.
[Image of Greco-Roman temple of Ras el Soda]

The temple is a prostyle temple, meaning that it has a portico with four columns at the front. The columns are Corinthian, which is one of the three classical orders of architecture. The temple is made of limestone with marble columns.

The cella, or inner chamber, of the temple is small and contains a niche where the statue of Isis would have been placed. The temple also has a second chamber, which may have been used for storage or as a living space for the priests.

The Ras el Soda temple is a unique example of Greco-Roman architecture in Egypt. It is also an important archaeological site because it provides insights into the religious practices of the people of Alexandria during the Roman period.

The temple was rebuilt in 1960 at its current location, near the Bibliotheca Alexandrina. Today, it is a popular tourist attraction and can be visited by the public.can

Matajer Mall might not be the biggest shopping center around, but it definitely stands out for how well-organized, clean, and comfortable it is. From the moment you walk in, you’re greeted with a calm and tidy atmosphere — no overwhelming crowds, no loud noise, just a smooth and pleasant place to shop or spend time.

The layout of the mall is simple and easy to navigate. The lighting is soft, the air conditioning is consistent, and everything feels clean and well-maintained. It’s the kind of place where you can actually enjoy walking around without feeling rushed or stressed.

There’s a decent variety of stores inside — clothing, cosmetics, electronics, home goods, and more. Most of the shops lean towards practical and affordable options, which makes it great for everyday shopping. While it doesn’t have a huge range of international luxury brands, what it does offer feels curated and useful. There are also a few local businesses that give the mall a bit of a community vibe.

The food court and cafes might not be massive, but they’re cozy and well-kept. Whether you’re in the mood for a quick bite or a coffee break, you’ll find something satisfying. One thing that stands out is how clean the dining areas are, and the staff in most spots are friendly and helpful.

Parking is usually easy to find, and the mall’s location makes it convenient to reach whether you’re driving or using public transportation. Security is present but discreet, which adds to the sense of safety without being intrusive.

Overall, Matajer Mall offers a calm and pleasant alternative to the crowded mega-malls. It’s a solid choice for running errands, grabbing a coffee, or doing a bit of light shopping in a relaxed setting. If you’re looking for a peaceful place to shop without the chaos, this mall definitely delivers.

Beautiful place for a relaxing day in Alexandria! 🌿 El Montazah Gardens has stunning greenery, sea views, and a peaceful atmosphere that feels like an escape from the city. Perfect for a walk, photos, or just enjoying the breeze. A classic Alexandria spot that’s definitely worth visiting. …

One of the most unique landmarks in Alexandria, Egypt. The Gardens were used to be the summerhouse for the Royal Family back at the time. Its main palace is used for presidential ceremonies only and inaccessible for public. The other two palaces are converted into hotels now. The entrance fee for a foreigner is USD10 or its equivalent in EGP paid by card or in cash; including access to the whole Gardens, the Royal Train, the Royal Greenhouse, and a soft drink at the Beach Club. Still, the Tea Kiosk has its own fee to enter including your choice of a black or green tea inside. Private cars aren’t allowed inside the premises, so you have to park in a paid car parking (EGP50 per car). Still, you can explore the Gardens by a paid golf cart, rent a bicycle to ride, or you may simply walk on foot around the Gardens. A must visit whenever you land in Alexandria!

Decent park, good open space in a fairly narrow district like Kafr Abdu, but not well taken care of and in need of good maintenance and renovation.

The whole district was named Allenby after the well known British Field Marshal Edmund Allenby, who had a residence and military presence in the area during the British occupation of Egypt.

However in October 1951 during a wave of nationalist sentiment and armed resistance in the Suez Canal cities, the Egyptian government renamed the district from “Allenby” to “Kafr Abdu”.

The new name was a tribute to a small village called Kafr Abdu, located in Ismailia Governorate, which became a symbol of resistance.

Residents of Kafr Abdu village refused to hand over Egyptian fedayeen (freedom fighters) to the British forces.

The village came under violent British attack but became a national emblem of bravery and resistance.

This Amphitheatre is one of its kind to be found in the Egypt. The entry fee to this place is 200 EGP. Excavations at the site were initially undertaken in search of the grave of Alexander the Great, however the 4th century Ancient Roman theatrewas uncovered instead. The ruins found included the original Roman marble seating, a number of courtyard mosaics, and even graffiti relating to the rivalry of supporters of local chariot teams. As well as the theatre itself, there are also the remains of a baths complex on the site and several other chambers and living quarters. Further research and excavations are still being carried out, with these finds shedding new light on the complex. Some of the latest theories are centred around the idea that the theatre was actually a small lecture hall, and that the complex as a whole was an academic institution – perhaps even an ancient university linked to the Great Library of Alexandria.

🌟 Serapeum of Alexandria – A Sacred Space Echoing Through Time
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

We visited the Serapeum of Alexandria and were completely moved by its quiet, ancient energy. Though the original temple no longer stands, the site is incredibly powerful—a must-see for any history lover visiting Alexandria.

The standout feature is Pompey’s Pillar—a towering red granite column that dominates the landscape and gives you a sense of the temple’s former grandeur. Around it, you can explore ruins, underground chambers, statues, and remnants of what was once a major center of learning and worship.

🧱 Why It’s Worth a Visit:
•	Walk through the underground galleries and ruins that once belonged to the temple of Serapis.
•	Learn about the fascinating history of the Serapeum as a spiritual and cultural crossroads blending Greek and Egyptian traditions.
•	The site also once held part of the Library of Alexandria’s “daughter collection.”

📸 Don’t miss your chance to stand beside Pompey’s Pillar and reflect on what once stood here—it’s a humbling and beautiful moment.

📍 Tip: Bring water, wear comfortable shoes, and arrive early to avoid the afternoon sun. If possible, hire a guide or do a little research ahead of time—there’s so much layered history here that signage doesn’t fully explain.

For us, this was a peaceful and deeply moving part of our Alexandria journey—highly recommended.

— Local Guide, ancient-site wanderer, and lover of forgotten corners

The Anfushi Tombs are among the most significant and oldest archaeological burial sites in Alexandria, not far from the Citadel of Qaitbay, but in a relatively isolated location near Ras El-Tin Palace.

The tombs date back to the Ptolemaic and early Roman periods, specifically around the 2nd and 1st centuries BC. They were first discovered in 1901, with more uncovered in later excavations.

They were used as burial sites for wealthy and noble Alexandrians during the Ptolemaic era. They reflect a fusion of Egyptian and Greek artistic styles, showing the multicultural nature of ancient Alexandria.

The tombs consist of underground chambers carved into the rock, accessed through stairways leading to elaborately decorated burial rooms.

However, the site is in dire conditions and very neglected, and it’s not even on many of the city’s touristic maps. It’s unfortunate because it’s more beautiful and preserved than Mustafa Kamel and Shatby sites.

The Greek Orthodox Cemetery in Alexandria, Egypt, is an important monument to the Greek community that settled in the city during the 19th and 20th centuries. The architecture of the cemetery is impressive, with ornate marble tombstones and family tombs that reflect the rich tradition of the Greek Orthodox community. Today, the cemetery is a place of historical memory and cultural heritage, keeping alive the connection between the Greek diaspora and the city of Alexandria.

Alexandria Naval Unknown Soldier Memorial
This monument stands on the Corniche in Mansheya and commemorates unknown naval soldiers who died at sea. The structure was originally built in the late 19th century (c. 1860s–1870s) by Alexandria’s Italian community to honor Khedive Ismail during Egypt’s period of modernization.

Following the Egyptian Revolution of 1952, its purpose was changed, and in 1964 it was officially rededicated as a memorial to unidentified naval personnel who lost their lives in maritime conflicts.

Located facing the Mediterranean, the monument reflects Alexandria’s long history as Egypt’s primary naval port, particularly during the 19th century under Muhammad Ali and later periods of military significance.

Today it serves as a public memorial space symbolizing remembrance, maritime history, and the city’s enduring connection to the sea.

Visiting the Qaitbay Citadel in Alexandria was an unforgettable experience and one of the highlights of my trip to Egypt. This impressive fortress sits proudly at the edge of the Mediterranean Sea, built on the exact site of the ancient Lighthouse of Alexandria — one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The combination of history, architecture, and breathtaking sea views makes it a must-visit destination.

As soon as I arrived, I was struck by the citadel’s grand stone walls and towers. The structure is remarkably well-preserved, and walking through its halls feels like stepping back into the 15th century. Inside, there are several chambers, narrow passageways, and lookout points where you can almost imagine soldiers standing guard centuries ago. The museum displays inside give a good overview of the citadel’s history and its role in protecting Egypt’s coastline.

The highlight for me was climbing to the upper levels and taking in the panoramic view of the sea and the city of Alexandria. The sound of the waves crashing against the rocks below creates an incredible atmosphere of peace and strength.

The site is clean, well maintained, and easy to explore at your own pace. I recommend visiting in the late afternoon to catch the sunset — the light reflecting off the stone walls and the water is absolutely magical.

Whether you’re a history lover, a photographer, or simply looking for a beautiful coastal view, Qaitbay Citadel is a must-see.

· Design: It features a square main tower with four circular corner towers, surrounded by two layers of defensive walls containing barracks and storage rooms.

WHERE HISTORY MEETS A SUNDAY EVENING - AN ALEXANDRIAN MOMENT AT QAITBAY

Our visit to the Citadel of Qaitbay in Alexandria on a Sunday evening turned out to be as much a social experience as a historical one. The area around the citadel was alive with local families enjoying their weekend by the sea. There was laughter, conversation, and an unmistakable sense of ease—Alexandrians unwinding in the salty Mediterranean breeze. The atmosphere was warm and festive, a reminder that monuments often live as much in the present as they do in the past.

One especially touching moment was meeting a local Muslim family—mostly women—celebrating the birthday of a little girl named Ameen. Amid a centuries-old fortress and timeless seascape, there was cake, smiles, and quiet joy. It was a small but powerful illustration of how historic spaces continue to serve as communal gathering points, even when their original purpose has long faded.

Historically, the citadel stands on hallowed ground. It occupies the very site where the legendary Lighthouse of Alexandria, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, once guided ships safely into the harbour. Built in the 15th century as a defensive fort, the citadel later guarded Egypt’s Mediterranean coast for centuries, bearing witness to shifting empires and evolving warfare.

In its present form, the citadel is no longer in active use. Interestingly, we noticed that relatively few visitors ventured inside the structure itself; most seemed content to linger outside, soaking in the sea views and the lively ambience. Perhaps that, too, is part of its modern significance. Today, the Citadel of Qaitbay functions less as a fortress and more as a backdrop—where Alexandria’s layered history quietly coexists with everyday life, leisure, and human connection.

The center and heart of Alexandria, Raml Station district is one of the liveliest districts in the city.

Known for its rich history, architectural elegance, and vibrant atmosphere, it has long served as a cultural, social, and transportation hub of the city.

The name “Raml” (Arabic for “sand”) comes from the area’s origins as a sandy village located on the eastern outskirts of Alexandria.

When the Alexandria tram system began operation in 1863, the station that served this village became known as “El Raml Station”, cementing the name.

In the late 19th century, during the reign of Khedive Abbas Hilmi II, Italian architect Antonio Lasciac designed the square in 1887 in a European style, surrounding it with elegant buildings resembling Florentine architecture.

The area is surrounded by historic cafés, restaurants, bookstores, old cinemas, the Chamber of Commerce, and the main post office.

It has been a gathering point for famous literary and artistic figures such as: Constantine Cavafy, Lawrence Durrell, E.M. Forster, Jean Cocteau and even international celebrities like Elvis Presley, Agatha Christie, and Muhammad Ali Clay are said to have passed through.

It’s not just a square, it’s a living museum of Alexandria’s cosmopolitan past and vibrant present.

Raml Station is a vibrant and historic part of Alexandria, showcasing a blend of colonial architecture, bustling city life, and local authenticity. Narrow alleys with laundry-draped balconies and vintage cars give it a nostalgic charm, though signs of urban wear are clearly visible.

Highlights:
•	Cultural landmarks such as the mosque with its beautiful minaret and the central square with its statue offer a sense of history and civic pride.
•	Local life is very present—street vendors, small shops, and pedestrians bring the area to life, making it feel authentically Egyptian.
•	Architectural diversity: From grand colonial facades to weathered mid-century buildings, there’s visual interest at every corner.

Challenges:
•	Urban decay is visible in many buildings, with some in need of restoration.
•	Cleanliness varies; some side streets have scattered trash.
•	Traffic and noise may be overwhelming during peak hours.

Ideal for:
Travelers interested in history, street photography, or experiencing the unpolished charm of an old Egyptian city center.

He played a key role in the Egyptian Revolution of 1919, as well as played a role in prompting the British Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence in 1922.

LIVING BEACON OF KNOWLEDGE ON THE MEDITERRANEAN

Our visit to Bibliotheca Alexandrina on a Sunday morning in January 2026 was one of the most intellectually stimulating experiences of our Egypt tour. As part of a large group, we spent nearly two hours exploring this magnificent institution and were struck immediately by its bold architecture and contemporary vision of what a library can be. We bought the entrance tickets in advance and the entry was smooth. Please note that the library generally discourages use of ‘sticks’ and ‘tripods’ for photos and videos.

Unlike traditional libraries dominated by shelves of printed volumes, the Bibliotheca is a digital knowledge hub. Hundreds of computer terminals were in constant use by students and scholars, accessing vast digital collections with quiet intensity. The atmosphere conveyed not silence alone, but focused intellectual energy.

Equally fascinating was learning about its historical inspiration—the legendary ancient Library of Alexandria, tragically lost to fire and destruction. Anecdotes about how ships entering ancient Alexandria were searched for books, which were copied before being returned, vividly illustrated the city’s insatiable thirst for knowledge. That spirit is clearly alive here.

Brief casual interactions with a couple  international students further enriched our visit. They spoke passionately about how indispensable the library is to Alexandria’s academic community—as a place for research, collaboration, and global exchange of ideas. I honestly felt that a 5 minute film about the library to the visitors would have been very useful. Maybe there is already a facility…but frankly I did not come across one.

Personally, I have never encountered anything quite like this in my lifetime. The visit was a profound learning experience and deeply inspiring. For anyone who values acquiring, sharing, and disseminating knowledge, this is an absolute must-visit. Kudos to Alexandria—truly a timeless Knowledge City.

The Library of Alexandria is one of the most famous cultural landmarks in Egypt and the world. It's located on the Mediterranean coast in the city of Alexandria.

The Bibliotheca Alexandrina is not just a landmark, but an experience that unfolds gradually the more time you give it. Even before entering, the exterior sets the tone: the massive circular structure, tilted toward the Mediterranean, feels both modern and symbolic. One detail you absolutely shouldn’t miss is the outer wall scripts—heading to B1 near the Planetarium entrance gives you the best view of the engraved alphabets and symbols carved into the stone, a powerful reminder of the library’s universal ambition.
Entry can be slightly confusing at first. The ticket offices are located on the opposite side from the ocean-facing façade, and the walk to get there is longer than it initially appears. When we arrived, we were directed to a specific window to pay by credit card, which worked fine but is something to keep in mind. Small logistical details aside, the process is straightforward once you’re in the right place.
Inside, the main reading hall is breathtaking in scale and design. It’s one of those spaces that makes you slow down instinctively. On the ground level, don’t rush past the details—one easily overlooked highlight is the Shakespeare couch, which took me a moment to fully understand, especially without my glasses. It’s subtle, clever, and very much in the spirit of the building.
Much of the artistic content—paintings, sculptures, and garments—is located on the B1 basement level, which is well worth exploring. This level adds cultural depth to the visit and balances the grandeur of the main hall with more intimate exhibits.
Overall, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina rewards patience and curiosity. It’s a place where architecture, history, and culture intersect, and whether you’re there for photos, learning, or quiet observation, it leaves a strong and lasting impression.
Tips:
Before going inside, take time to see the outer wall scripts by heading to B1 near the Planetarium entrance — they’re easy to miss and worth the walk.
The ticket offices are on the opposite side from the ocean-facing façade, and getting there involves a longer walk than expected.
If paying by credit card, you may be directed to a specific ticket window, so don’t be surprised if not all counters handle card payments.
The majority of the artworks (paintings, sculptures, garments) are located on the B1 basement level, so don’t skip it.
Inside the main library hall, explore the ground level slowly and look for details like the Shakespeare couch, which is subtle and easy to misunderstand at first glance.
Wear comfortable shoes — the complex is large and involves a lot of walking.

Tiramisu Croffle

First off, let me say I love the atmosphere here. It is quiet, it is clean, and its colours play very well together. Their design blend of Scandinavian minimalism and Renaissance boutique is very charming, and reflects the newly refurbished Fouad Street well.

However, I must unfortunately say, their croffle, which is their prized item, was the lowlight of this experience.

The tiramisu croffle was the only one they offered that day, and boy, was it a disappointment. The croissant base was cold, soggy, and stale. Its outer crust had no flake or crunch, but was rather leathery, and its inside collapsed in on itself. Any buttery flavour the croissant had to offer was instantly ruined by an inexplicable bitter aftertaste (Most likely the cocoa powder burning on reheat, something the savoirdi suffered as well).

This was miserable as a croissant, as a waffle, and as a food item of its own accord. I understand these desserts are brought in overnight and then reheated, but this felt like it was week-old, frozen meshaltet pie that was pulled out of the freezer and placed into a microwave.

The tiramisu cream was serviceable, I will give them that, and had some signature tang despite looking like whipped cream.

As for the coffee, it had no flavour at all. So I will not include it in my rating.

Love the idea, love the decor, hate the implementation. For the price they charge, I cannot recommend them in good conscience. I hope they eventually get the formula down!

Ambience & Setting

Jeeda’s offers a vibrant, warm atmosphere that perfectly captures the “Chiringuito” (Spanish beach bar) spirit. The decor is rustic yet chic, making it one of the most stylish spots in Alexandria. Whether you’re sitting inside with the cozy lighting or enjoying the sea breeze, the vibe is energetic and upscale.

The Food

• La Del Mar Pizza: A standout choice. The crust is thin and airy with a perfect char, topped with fresh seafood that reminds you you’re right by the Mediterranean.
• Paella: Authentic and rich in flavor. The rice had a great texture, though the highlight was the depth of the saffron-infused broth.
• Solomillo a la Brasa: The star of the meal. Perfectly grilled tenderloin with a smoky finish that melts in your mouth.
• Churros Madrileño: The ideal ending. Crispy, golden, and served with a rich chocolate dip—exactly how they’re done in Madrid.

Service & Staff

The staff is attentive and well-versed in the menu (we had mimo but they’re all great). They manage the pace of the meal well, ensuring the tapas and mains don’t arrive all at once, which allows for a relaxed dining experience.

Seaside is easily one of the best seafood restaurants in Alexandria. Personally, my favorite. It’s always where I have my first lunch every time I’m in Alexandria.

The view is unbeatable, especially from the beautiful upper terrace overlooking the water. Whether you sit indoors or outside, the whole experience feels special because of the setting.

The service is excellent. Supervisors and staff are always attentive, present and genuinely on the lookout for guests. You never feel like you’re searching for someone, there is always staff nearby, happy to help and quick to respond, which makes a huge difference.

A special mention to Osama and Abubaker for their amazing service and hospitality. Honestly, the whole team as well, from the kitchen to the waiters to the cleaning staff. Professional, welcoming and always attentive, they truly add to the experience and reflect the standard of the place.

The food is amazing and consistently cooked to perfection. It is always served at the right time, properly hot, and with real consistency in quality. I’ve even asked for small adjustments to salads based on my preference, and they handled it beautifully. The clams are my favorite, and they are always properly cleaned with no sand at all and perfectly cooked, which says a lot in a seafood restaurant. The salads are fresh, the bread is excellent, and everything is served properly.

What I also appreciate is that despite being a seafood restaurant with fresh fish on display, the place never has that strong seafood smell some places struggle with. It stays clean, fresh and comfortable, which says a lot about their standards.

1. Stuffed pigeon

3. Mixed salad
4. One tea
5. 330 ml water

Attached are images of both the bill and the exquisite food I enjoyed during my visit.

As a tourist, feeling welcomed and treated fairly is essential to a positive dining experience. I urge Ebn El Balad Restaurant to consider this matter and ensure transparency in their pricing practices to uphold their reputation as a welcoming establishment for all visitors.

We ordered Marinara Pizza, Spinach Ravioli, Mozzarella Bruschetta and Blue Mojito for dinner. The only thing we could possibly complain about was the bruschetta arriving at the same time as the food, as we had assumed it would come first.

*Marinara pizza* was perfect to all extends. Nicely evenly cooked dough, saucy but not mushy, chewy and crunchy. We are planning on ordering pizza from here more often.

*Spinach and cheese ravioli* Great. I couldn’t exactly tell from the texture if it was frozen or not, but they really made it well enough for the flavors to pop up. I love some spinach ravioli and was not let down.

*Mozzarella Bruschetta* Probably the weakest part of the meal, still being very good. The ingredients were great, specifically the cherry tomatoes that were cooked “al dente”, bread was crispy and clearly fresh.

*Blue mojito* I guess this one would be a basic syrup mix like in other restaurants, but the fresh lemon and the perfect amount of ice really fulfilled the atmosphere. Lovely drink choice. - Apologies, as I forgot to take a picture of the drink. We were too excited about the pizza taste…

Overall this restaurant gave us a nice experience which we mean to repeat. Made me feel at home, with a comfortable environment, service and most importantly great meal.

As a tourist in Alexandria, I attempted to book a table at Skyroof (Windsor Palace Hotel). My experience during the reservation process was nothing short of disgraceful for a hotel of this reputation.

​During my inquiry via Instagram and a subsequent phone call, I was denied a reservation because I am a German man accompanied by an Egyptian male friend. I was told the venue is only open to 'couples' or 'mixed groups.' In an international city like Alexandria, such blatant discrimination based on gender and companionship is completely unacceptable and feels discriminatory.

​The situation escalated when I spoke to the management:

​Lack of Professionalism: The lady on the phone refused to give her name, which is unheard of in high-end hospitality. ​Shocking Arrogance: When I mentioned that I would leave a public review about this treatment, she mockingly replied that she didn't care at all about negative ratings on Google or TripAdvisor. This level of indifference towards guests is toxic to the hotel's reputation. ​Broken Promises: Despite promising to pass my number to the higher management for a callback, I was ignored.

​It is a shame that such a historic landmark is run by people who treat guests with such disrespect and apply outdated, discriminatory policies. I strongly advise any traveler to avoid this place. There are plenty of wonderful alternatives in Alexandria that actually value hospitality and equality.

​Bottom line: Reservation denied due to discriminatory rules, followed by an incredibly arrogant management. A total embarrassment!"

Tolip Hotel Alexandria is honestly one of the best hotel experiences I’ve had in the city. It’s not just a hotel, it really feels like a full destination suitable for the whole family, regardless of age.
I booked a suite, and it completely exceeded my expectations. It was huge, with two very spacious bedrooms, one with a queen-size bed and the other with two double beds. The mattresses were extremely comfortable, and we all slept very well. The suite also included two full bathrooms, which made things very convenient.
The living area was massive, featuring two sofas, four armchairs, and a small round dining table for four. There were also three TVs, with a large one in the living room. Storage was more than enough, with large wardrobes and cabinets in each room. On top of that, the suite came with three balconies offering stunning views of both the sea and the swimming pool. Sitting on the balcony facing the sea was easily one of the highlights of the stay.
Getting around the hotel was also very smooth. There are four elevators, and despite the hotel being quite busy, we never had to wait long.
The breakfast experience was good, around a strong 4 stars. There’s a huge variety of food, and most of it was delicious. The restaurant itself is located on the 11th floor with a beautiful sea view, which makes the experience even better. However, the organization and cleanliness of the tables and floors could definitely be improved, and some of the buffet equipment felt a bit outdated. Still, I highly recommend booking with breakfast, as it offers great value compared to alternatives in Alexandria.
The swimming pool was excellent, with professional and helpful lifeguards, and towels provided directly at the pool.
What really sets this hotel apart are the “hidden gems” that not many people know about:

Private Beach Access: There’s a private beach with a free, air-conditioned shuttle bus running every hour from the hotel entrance, and returning every half hour until around 5:30 PM. While the beach itself is not very large and the sea isn’t perfect, everything else is great, free towels, very clean bathrooms, shaded seating, and a café with reasonably priced drinks.
Cinema: The hotel has two cinema theaters showing relatively new movies, with tickets at a very affordable price (around 100 EGP).
Entertainment Room: Includes billiards and table tennis at reasonable prices.
Large Lobby Area: Plenty of comfortable seating to relax or meet with others.
Spa Facilities: Includes massage services, jacuzzi, sauna, and hot tub, all at reasonable prices.
Nearby Options: Within walking distance, there are well-known fast-food options like KFC, Pizza Hut, and Hardee’s, plus a grocery store for essentials.

Overall, Tolip Hotel offers incredible value, spacious and comfortable accommodations, great facilities, and plenty of activities. Despite a few minor issues with breakfast organization, I would highly recommend it for anyone visiting Alexandria.

I write this review with a constructive purpose — to help improve a hotel that once delivered a wonderful experience. I stayed here 10 years ago and still remember the quality, which makes the current decline especially disappointing.

Cons
- Unacceptable construction noise: Construction — officially 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM — started earlier, disturbing guests.
- No sound-isolation: There is no proper sound insulation — you can hear street traffic and car horns loudly at night, making it almost impossible to sleep or rest peacefully. This is a major comfort issue.
- Outdated room access experience: Only one physical key per room; it broke and I was told to wait the entire night until a replacement was made — unacceptable for any modern hospitality standard.
- Poor Wi-Fi with outdated policy: Internet is limited to 1GB per person, and barely functions on high floors. In the modern age, unlimited reliable internet is a basic necessity for all travelers — for work, communication, safety, and planning.
- Rooms lack maintenance: Outdated furniture, worn fixtures, and neglected facilities.
- Cleanliness concerns: Dust and lack of proper preparation upon check-in.
- Strange room-service policy: No glass cups provided — only small cardboard cups, something I have never encountered worldwide.

⚠️ A Key Point – Not Just a Renovation Problem
The biggest concern is that many issues reflect management policies and mindset, not just an old building. Wi-Fi limits, lack of spare keys, cardboard cups, failure to enforce quiet hours, and construction starting early — these are operational decisions that actively harm the hotel’s brand.
An old hotel can still feel premium — but when policies communicate cost-cutting over guest comfort, the reputation collapses.

Pros
+ Beautiful sea view: The triple room’s sea view is truly exceptional.
+ Some staff members genuinely tried to help, and their efforts are appreciated such as Waleed El Sayed so thanks for your individual efforts.

Final Message
This review is written because I care. Kaoud once offered a memorable experience. With leadership improvements, updated guest-centered policies, proper sound-proofing, and renovation, it can recover its past greatness. I hope this message is received as a call to restore Kaoud Hotel to the standard it once proudly held.

This magnificent and majestic hotel is situated on the sea front with the most beautiful views from the room and from the roof top restaurant.  It used to be a king's palace and was converted to a hotel in 1906.

Upon entering I felt like I was in a 1950's film.  It was like being transported back in time.

The security staff at the entrance were accommodating and so kind towards us.  A special thanks to the very tall Mohamed and the rest of the staff.

Also thanks to the lovely staff at reception - Ahmed, Youssef & Reem.

Another special thanks to Ahmed who bought our suitcases up to us & got us a taxi & who was very kind and helpful & to Amr Ibrahim who got us a taxi as well and for his kindness too.

An extra special thanks to the lovely,  kind & knowledgeable Christina from Guest Relations who gave us a very warm welcome to the hotel that included a flower for me & the most delicious mini macarons,  biscuits and other pastries. We also had a delicious complimentary Hibiscus juice & more biscuits on the night before we left.

On our departure day, we met Meena, also from guest relations,  who was so lovely and kind as well.

Thanks too to.all the housekeeping staff for their hard work.

The lift is old fashioned and thrilling to go in.  First there is a security gate and then you open the door on.both sides.

Our room was spacious and clean with a breath taking view of the sea and city. We also had a small but adequate balcony. The bathroom was clean and super too.

The Blue Harbour rooftop is wonderful. The staff are accommodating,  kind and lovely.  The food is fresh and delicious.  The shrimp caesar salad is the best as is the Lebanese mezze starter. The Sunshine (7 up and cherry syrup) and the Sunrise (7 up, lemon, grenadine syrup) cocktails are refreshing and yum.

My best was the Breakfast Buffet.  A huge variety of cereals, best cooked oats, fruit salad, yoghurt, hot foods that include yummy chicken sausages and beef too, foul mesdames, potato, hard boiled eggs etc,  then the lovely Chef Kareem makes delicious omelettes, thete is an Oriental breakfast too...cheeses,  cold meats, salads etc & saving the best for last is the breads, baguettes,  croissant, assortment of pastries & the most delicious mini plain & chocolate pancakes filled with a custard. Yum cappuccino too.

If you would like exceptional and precious staff,  mouth watering foods and  beautiful sea views, I urge you to stay at this hotel. Highly recommended

Saint George Church in Sporting, Alexandria, is one of the most spiritually alive and blessed churches in the city. It is not just a place of worship, but a true spiritual home where love, peace, and warmth are deeply felt from the moment you enter ⛪🕊️.

This blessed church is closely connected with the life and service of Fr. Bishoy Kamel, one of the most beloved and influential Coptic Orthodox priests of modern times. Fr. Bishoy Kamel was a living example of a faithful priest, known for his humility, deep love, and sincere care for every person, especially the youth and those in need 💒❤️.
Fr. Bishoy Kamel was born in 1931 and graduated from the Faculty of Science before dedicating his life fully to priestly service. He was well known for his simple yet profound teachings, his strong emphasis on personal pastoral care, and his belief that a true priest carries his people in his heart before God 🙏🔥. He departed in peace in 1979, but his spiritual legacy continues to inspire generations.
Visiting Saint George Church in Sporting is a rich spiritual experience, filled with prayer, love, and the blessings of Saint George and the holy life of Fr. Bishoy Kamel. I highly recommend this church to anyone seeking true peace, spiritual growth, and a deeper relationship with God ✝️🕊️.

The Sails in Motion Statue
This famous statue is located in front of the Library of Alexandria in Silsila Square in the Azarita district of Alexandria. It was created by the Egyptian sculptor Fathi Mahmoud in 1962. The statue depicts a beast with the head of a bull and a body undulating like the sea, embracing a beautiful woman resembling a mermaid. The statue incorporates the story of the creation of Alexandria through an ancient myth about the sea god, sometimes represented as a bull, who has a firm grip on a beautiful girl symbolizing Alexandria.

Our visit to the Planetarium Science Center came naturally after exploring the Bibliotheca Alexandrina and the museum of antiquities, as these form a seamless cultural and intellectual complex. We visited around noon on a weekend in January 2026, also as a part of a big group and spent about half an hour here—just enough to appreciate its purpose and atmosphere.
Located right on the shores of the Mediterranean and in close proximity to the new Library Complex, the Planetarium Science Center enjoys a superb setting, with open plazas, sea breeze, and palm-lined walkways enhancing the experience even before stepping inside. The striking semi-circular dome, symbolic of the heavens, immediately signals that this is a space dedicated to science and discovery.
Inside, the focus is clearly on communication of science and technology rather than traditional exhibits. The digital planetarium is one of the main attractions, offering immersive presentations on astronomy, space, and Earth sciences. Even with limited time, it is evident that the centre is designed especially for students and young learners, with interactive displays and an engaging, hands-on approach. I would have appreciated if there were more people around to guide us around.
The centre also hosts lectures, workshops, and special events, making it a lively complement to the more contemplative library next door. Compact, modern, and purpose-driven, the Planetarium Science Center adds a contemporary scientific dimension to Alexandria’s historic role as a city of knowledge—well worth a short, focused visit after the library. Maybe I should have visited the entire complex (notably Bibliotheca Alexandrina) when I was a young student. Never mind. Better late than never.

The Alexandria Corniche is a scenic waterfront promenade that stretches along the Mediterranean coastline of Alexandria, Egypt. The term "Corniche" is commonly used to refer to a road or promenade along the waterfront, providing stunning views of the sea and often lined with parks, gardens, and recreational areas. The Alexandria Corniche is a popular destination for both locals and tourists, offering a relaxing atmosphere and beautiful vistas. Here are some key features and attractions associated with the Alexandria Corniche:

Mediterranean Sea Views: One of the main attractions of the Corniche is its panoramic views of the Mediterranean Sea. Visitors can enjoy the sea breeze and take in the sight of the waves crashing against the shore.

Landmarks: The Corniche is dotted with landmarks and notable buildings, including historic structures and modern developments. It's a picturesque area where visitors can explore the city's architectural and cultural heritage.

Gardens and Parks: Some sections of the Corniche are adorned with gardens and parks, providing green spaces for relaxation and leisure activities. These areas may include walking paths, benches, and recreational facilities.

Restaurants and Cafes: Along the Corniche, there are often restaurants and cafes where visitors can enjoy local and international cuisine while taking in the waterfront views.

Recreational Activities: The promenade is a popular place for walking, jogging, and cycling. Many people visit the Corniche for recreational activities and to enjoy a leisurely stroll along the waterfront.

Sunsets: The Alexandria Corniche is particularly renowned for offering spectacular sunset views over the Mediterranean. It's a favorite spot for those who want to witness the sun setting over the sea.

The Nabi Daniel Mosque in Alexandria is a historic mosque . It is tomb of Prophet Daniel and Luqman al-Hakeem, a wise man mentioned in the Quran.

- *Architecture*: The mosque has a rectangular area surrounded by an open courtyard, with ablution facilities and separate restrooms for males and females.
- *Tomb Chamber*: A staircase leads down to the basement, where two tombs are present, one attributed to Muhammad Daniyal al-Mawsili and the other to Luqman al-Hakeem.
- *History*: The mosque has undergone several transformations, with some speculating it might be the site of Alexander the Great's tomb due to its underground vaults and passages.¹

- Visitors can perform solat (prayer) in the mosque and explore the tomb chamber.
- The mosque's location in the heart of Alexandria makes it easily accessible.

- *Local Legend*: The mosque is believed by some to be the final resting place of Prophet Daniel.

- *Pedestrian-Friendly Street*: The street leading to the mosque is closed to vehicles, making it a pleasant walk for visitors.
- *Beautifully Paved*: The street is well-maintained and paved, adding to the area's charm.
- *Lined with Shops*: Local shops line the street, offering visitors a glimpse into the local culture and economy.
- *Local Feeling*: Visitors can immerse themselves in the local atmosphere by taking a leisurely stroll through the street.

Ancient Canopic Way (Alexandria)
The Canopic Way was the principal east–west avenue of ancient Alexandria, established around 331 BCE after the city’s foundation by Alexander the Great and designed within a formal grid plan by Dinocrates of Rhodes. It formed one of the two main axes of the city, intersecting a north–south road and organizing Alexandria as a planned Hellenistic metropolis.

Named for its direction toward Canopus (east of Alexandria), the avenue functioned as the city’s central artery. Ancient accounts describe it as unusually wide (often estimated around 30 meters), lined with colonnades, statues, and major civic buildings. Along or near its course were key institutions of the Ptolemaic capital (3rd–1st centuries BCE), including royal quarters, temples, and the scholarly complex associated with the Library of Alexandria.

Under Roman rule (from 30 BCE), the Canopic Way remained a focal route for administration, movement, and ceremonial processions. It continued in use into late antiquity, though earthquakes, subsidence, and repeated rebuilding gradually obscured and buried much of the original city fabric between roughly the 4th–8th centuries CE.

Today, no visible continuous remains of the Canopic Way survive. However, its alignment is thought to correspond broadly with parts of modern central Alexandria, including areas near Fouad Street and Raml Station. Walking these streets follows, in approximate terms, the same urban spine that structured Alexandria for over a millennium.

The Canopic Way is significant not as a preserved monument, but as the underlying framework of the ancient city—linking political power, intellectual life, and daily activity across one of the Mediterranean’s most important historical centers.

One of the oldest mosques in Alexandria.

The mosque originally stood on the site of the Church of Saint Athanasius, built around 370 AD. After the Islamic conquest of Egypt in 641 AD, the church was converted into a mosque. This early mosque was known as Al-Attarine Mosque, also referred to historically as the Eastern Mosque.

In 1084 AD (477 AH), the mosque was completely rebuilt by the famous Fatimid vizier Badr al-Jamali. It became a Friday mosque, reflecting its religious importance.

A major structural collapse occurred in 1370 AD (772 AH), which led to a partial renovation. However, attention to the mosque diminished in the following centuries.

In 1901 AD (1319 AH), Khedive Abbas Helmy II ordered a full reconstruction of the mosque. Today’s building largely dates from this period, although an original foundation inscription from Badr al-Jamali’s time still remains above the entrance.

One of the most overlooked landmarks in Alexandria that still stands as a testament of one of the most well known horrific stories in Egypt and the Arab World.

Raya and Sakina were two Egyptian sisters who became notorious serial killers in the early 20th century. Their crimes shocked Egypt and made headlines across the Arab world, turning them into figures of legend and fear.

Between 1919 and 1920, Raya and Sakina, along with their husbands and two male accomplices, lured women into their homes, mostly prostitutes, Jewelry sellers and women of rich backgrounds. The victims were intoxicated, strangled to death, their valuables stolen, then their bodies buried beneath the house in the basement. The total number of victims were 17.

What makes the story more crazy is that the house is located exactly next to a police station back then.

Police were tipped off after human remains were found beneath one of the houses the sisters had rented.

The trial was one of the most sensational in Egyptian legal history. In 1921, Raya and Sakina were convicted and sentenced to death. They became the first women to be executed by the modern Egyptian state.

Their story became a major part of the culture of Egyptian society and inspired multiple films, TV series, plays, and even a comedy version of their tale.

The Imam al-Busiri Mosque in Alexandria is located on the seafront in the Anfoushi district, in the area known as Midan al-Masajid (Mosque Square), opposite the Sidi al-Mursi Abu al-Abbas Mosque. Imam al-Busiri was born in the first of Shawwal in the year 608 AH (1213 CE) in the town of Dalas, where his mother was born. He grew up in Busir, an ancient village between Fayoum and Beni Suef, from which his father was also born. He became known as al-Busiri. He was a pious and devout scholar, famous for praising the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in many poems, the most famous of which is the Burda. Al-Busiri died in Alexandria in the year 694 AH (1295 CE).

The author of the Burda poem, Imam al-Busiri, praises the Prophet Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him). The poem, consisting of 164 verses, has been translated into several languages. Its author suffered from paralysis. After completing it, he saw the Prophet in a dream, who clothed him in his cloak. Upon waking, he was cured of his illness. The poem holds a high place in the literature of love and praise for the Prophet Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), a refined form of literature stemming from the love of hearts for him. Imam Sharaf al-Din Muhammad ibn Sa’id Al-Busiri was a celebrated Sufi poet from Egypt, best known for his famous poem “Al-Burda” (The Poem of the Mantle), in praise of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. His work gained immense popularity throughout the Muslim world and continues to be recited today.

He spent his final years in Alexandria, where he died and was buried. He was buried in a small zawiya (Sufi lodge) established by Yahya Pasha, a local official.

Under the rule of Khedive Said Pasha, the small zawiya was demolished and replaced with the current mosque building directly above the tomb. And in 1889, Khedive Tawfiq ordered further renovations to strengthen and beautify the mosque.

The mosque features calligraphy from Imam Al-Busiri’s “Burda” poem, especially verses in white text on deep blue background.

It’s a prominent destination for Sufis and for everyone who loves the famous Burda poem and many come to recite the Burda and many other Islamic remembrances next to the tomb.

The Basili Mosque is a mosque steeped in history and a story that reflects the Egyptian people. It was built by the Christian businessman Asaad Basili, considered one of the most influential figures in the timber industry. He revolutionized

In Pictures - "Basili Mosque": An Architectural Masterpiece Built by a Christian Beloved by Muslims

Basili Mosque (12)

Click here to see more photos

Alexandria - Mohamed El-Badry:

For decades, Egypt has known how its Christians and Muslims coexist, sometimes to the point of sharing similar customs and traditions. Amidst this, some have demonstrated tolerance in ways that exceeded expectations, most notably the story of the famous Basili family in Alexandria and the mosque that bears their name in the Wardian district of Mina El-Basal.

The mosque's history dates back to the Basili family, whose patriarch was the renowned businessman Asaad Pasha Basili, who enriched the Egyptian economy. His Christian faith did not prevent him from contributing to the mosque's construction out of respect for Islam in the 1950s.

Masrawy's camera toured the corners of the famous mosque, which still bears a sign with the name of its founder, and met with a number of local residents who witnessed its founding and shared their knowledge of this edifice, its founder, and the reason for its construction.

An Architectural Masterpiece

The moment you step inside the mosque, your eyes are inevitably drawn to a collection of Islamic decorations that retain their vibrant colors. These range from the inscriptions on the imam's pulpit and the reciter's chair, to the stained glass windows that allow sunlight to filter through and illuminate the entire prayer hall, culminating in the mosque's dome, whose design allows the Islamic motifs adorning its ceiling and surrounding area to be illuminated.

Dr. Islam Assem, head of the Alexandria Tourist Guides Syndicate, says that the mosque is an architectural masterpiece. While its exterior is simple, its interior is magnificent, with its marble and mosaic floors, mihrab, and walls. The pulpit and ceiling are constructed of carved wood inlaid with ivory, and the chandeliers, specially crafted for the mosque, are unique in their decorative style, employing openwork designs that highlight Quranic verses in a circular pattern.

The mosque is registered in the heritage register as a mosque with a distinctive architectural style, and it is highly likely that it was built by an Egyptian engineer, a student of the Italian architect Mario Rossi, according to the head of the guides' association.

A testament to tolerance

The head of the guides' association recounts the mosque's history, saying, "Alexandrian society was extremely harmonious and tolerant. Therefore, there was no conflict or sensitivity regarding religious matters, and this mosque is the greatest testament to the acceptance of others, harmonious coexistence, and the atmosphere of tolerance that prevailed in the city."

He adds that Asaad Pasha Basili saw it as being in the public interest to build a mosque for his workers and those residing in the vicinity of his company, as there was no mosque nearby. The people remembered his generosity and named the mosque after him, without complaint, even though the company's name changed after nationalization.

Hajj Abdo El-Erian, one of the mosque's early patrons and a witness to its opening in the 1950s, says: "This mosque was built on a plot of land donated by Asaad Pasha Basili from his timber company in the Wardian district. It was intended to serve the company's workers and the local residents, providing a place for them to pray throughout the day. At that time, the workers had to travel long distances to reach a mosque far from the area, and the company owner wanted to maintain the smooth operation of the mosque without interfering with the Muslims' religious practices."

The seventy-seven-year-old sheikh adds: "The greatest testament to this kind Coptic man's respect for Muslims is that he could have built a small prayer room or simply a simple prayer area requiring only a few rugs. Instead, he employed the most skilled architects of the time and used the finest architectural elements, comparable to the most prestigious mosques in Egypt. He also ensured ample space for landscaping, creating a beautiful facade that enhances the mosque's spiritual atmosphere."

Hajj Abdo points out that Asaad Basili did not witness the mosque's opening because he commissioned its construction and passed away before its completion. He adds that Asaad did not want the mosque named after him out of respect for Muslim sensibilities and preferred it to be called the "Timber Company Mosque." However, the mosque's attendees named it Basili in appreciation and pride for its builder.

The First Mawlid Celebration

Hajj Sayed Ibrahim, one of those present at the mosque's opening, also recounts the story, saying, "The Basili family demonstrated their respect for Muslims on more than one occasion. For example, they invited one of the most prominent Quran reciters in Egypt and the Middle East at that time to lead the Mawlid celebrations. The late Sheikh Abdul Basit Abdul Samad was invited to recite Quranic verses in a large tent in front of the mosque to accommodate the large crowds that came from all over."

Alexandrian dessert parlor, famous for its couscous, rice pudding, and ice cream.

Ordered: Rice pudding with nuts and ice cream.

This place might be the most revered dairy dessert shop among the Alexandrian population. Even hinting towards not having tried the establishment would make locals look at you with crazy eyes and recommend you try it at once.

To this day, they maintain their more vintage facade and interiors, but don’t let that fool you, for they hold up a very tight cleaning policy and keep the place spotless.

I am sad to say, however, that even my nostalgia couldn’t cloud my judgment when it comes to their dessert.

You see, Sheikh Wafeek uses milk ice cream for this dessert, plain milk. Not flavoured with mastic. Not flavoured with vanilla. Which, when added to a vessel of rice pudding, doesn’t add much flavour-wise.

Moreover, since their rice pudding skewed more runny than gelatinous, the melting ice cream failed to do much texture-wise either. All it did was add in a few intermittent chilled bites, which made the dish slightly more fun.

Surprisingly, the star of the show was the topping of nuts. It's quite a generous handful considering the price you pay, and they even throw in some pistachios, which in this economy is a rare practice.

Overall, I still found this quite a unique and enjoyable experience. I mean its ice cream and rice pudding, of course I loved it! But it was not quite the locals or my childhood memories made it out to be…

First, the restaurant is really busy so on weekends so make sure to go early. Sitting outside is a must, the view and atmosphere are amazing. You still get a sense of its Greek heritage with the blue and white tables.

Food wasn’t very late, and try to not fill up on dips, salads and bread because the seafood is amazing. Fish, shrimps, soups, rice…everything was really good.
A big unfortunate thing is the absence of alcohol on the menu which is a very big shame. A beer (or even ouzo) would have been amazing with this whole experience. I hope their management considers doing something about this.
Service wise, do not expect a five star service but overall the staff is rather nice.

Zephere Seafood in El-Max, Alexandria, is a well-known local spot with a charmingly old-school feel and a great seaside atmosphere. The moment you arrive, you can tell it’s a place that has been loved by locals for years. The location near the water gives it a unique vibe that sets the mood even before the food arrives.

The menu is very seafood-focused, offering a wide range of fresh options—from fish to shrimp to calamari. You can see the seafood displayed, which gives confidence in the freshness. The style is simple and authentic, sticking to Egyptian coastal flavors rather than anything overly fancy.

The food itself is generally enjoyable, especially if you like traditional Alexandria-style preparations. The seafood is grilled or fried well, though the flavors can sometimes feel a little basic if you’re used to more seasoned or modern dishes. Still, it captures the charm of classic Egyptian seafood cooking.

Service can be a bit rushed during busy times, especially on weekends, but the staff remain friendly and efficient. The pricing is reasonable for the quantity and freshness you get, though some dishes may feel slightly higher than expected depending on what you choose. The overall atmosphere, however, helps balance that out.

Zephere Seafood is definitely worth trying at least once for its iconic status and coastal charm. It’s a solid place to experience local seafood in Alexandria, even if it might not be a restaurant you find yourself returning to frequently. A great stop for anyone wanting a taste of authentic Egyptian seaside dining.

During our recent trip to Alexandria on 26th Dec, 5 of us dined at JamBooJo Sea Food, and it turned out to be one of the highlights of the journey.
The experience began by handpicking our fresh fish and jumbo prawns, setting the stage for what followed. Once seated, we were welcomed with complimentary drinks, followed by shrimp kofta and falafel, and even dessert on the house — a thoughtful and generous touch.
We ordered European sea bass (Qarous) and gilthead sea bream (Denis), both expertly grilled. Every bite was exceptional — delicately marinated so the natural flavour of the fish remained centre stage. The flesh was tender, flaky, and succulent, with a gentle char from the grill that added depth without overpowering the freshness. There was no hint of fishiness, only clean, ocean-fresh flavour that lingered beautifully on the palate.
The jumbo prawns, served butter-style and grilled, were equally memorable. Rich, juicy, and perfectly cooked, each bite delivered a sweet, buttery richness balanced by the smoky warmth of the grill — indulgent yet refined.
The ambience was beautiful and relaxed, allowing the food to shine while you fully enjoy the moment. This is seafood prepared with confidence, restraint, and respect for quality ingredients.
Highly recommended for anyone visiting Alexandria and looking for exceptional seafood, warm hospitality, and a truly satisfying dining experience. A place we would return to without hesitation.

The Montazah Palace Gardens are renowned, especially after the recent renovations that added areas such as the lakes, several restaurants, a parking lot, a tourist promenade in front of the palace and along the sea, a marina, and some roads. However, the roads are not yet suitable for even the golf carts used to transport passengers within the gardens. The Helnan Palestine Hotel is located directly on the sea, offering breathtaking views and 5-star service. The hotel has a private beach with water sports and jet skis, and yachts can be rented for sea excursions. There are two spacious mosques for worshippers, one near the train station gate and the other next to the hotel and palace. My stay at Triomphe Hotel was extremely disappointing from start to finish. It began with misleading information provided by the reservation staff. When I called to book a room, I was offered three categories: sea view for 600 EGP per night, tram view for 500 EGP per night, and skylight view for 400 EGP per night. However, upon arrival, the receptionist informed me that the tram view cost 600 EGP. When I mentioned that I was quoted 500 EGP, he insisted that it had always been 600 EGP, implying I was mistaken or lying.

Faced with the same price for both tram view and sea view, I opted for the sea view room. Before being escorted to my room, I specifically asked the receptionist if there were any chances of insects or rodents being present, due to my arachnophobia. He assured me that the rooms were thoroughly cleaned and sterilized regularly.

Upon entering the room, I was shocked to find the trash can full of garbage, unclean blankets, and a dirty floor. Although the housekeeping staff responded quickly to my request to re-clean the room, the initial state was unacceptable.

The worst part of my stay occurred at 4:30 AM. I felt something touch my shoulder while I was sleeping. Turning on the lights, I discovered a cockroach in the bed. Horrified, I went to the reception, where the staff member sprayed the room with insecticide. The smell was unbearable, and I couldn't sleep for the rest of the night due to both the fear of more insects and the overpowering chemical odor.

Overall, my experience at Triomphe Hotel was dreadful. The misinformation, poor room conditions, and presence of insects made my stay extremely unpleasant. I do not recommend this hotel to anyone and suggest looking elsewhere for accommodation.

When the pizza arrived, we informed another waiter about what had happened. He denied seeing the incident, even though several staff members were standing right next to the waiter at the time. Eventually, the waiter who handled the pizza admitted the mistake and offered to replace it.

Alexandrian Boulangerie and Cafe, situated near the University Hospital.

Ordered: Plain Croissant and Cappuccino

Let me begin by saying, this croissant was about as close to perfect as a croissant could get without being financially devastating. It was crispy, flaky, buttery, fluffy, and fresh, but cooled long enough to be edible and allow for a proper crust. Could it have used some sort of premium wheat sourdough? Sure, could it have been even butterier? It could always be. But let’s be fair, this is a very well-made croissant, even by artisanal standards.

The cappuccino was a proper cappuccino, with a respectable layer of foam that remained all the way to the end and left residue on the mug. Doesn’t sound like much? Well, it’s more than I can say for most of their competitors.

The atmosphere was quite exquisite. Decorated in a classy Renaissance chic and graced with thematic classical French tunes. Its view of the park is quite delightful, and the seating area, while quaint, was very well kept and ventilated.

Service was great too. The order came out fairly quickly, and my waiter was polite enough to inform me that my order was part of an Eid offer, which I wasn’t previously aware of.

All in all, I am glad I came here today, and recommend this boulangerie to croissant enthusiasts visiting the city.

Swedish burger chain, serving burgers, fries, and birria tacos.

Ordered: Double Cheeseburger

I’d been excited to come to this place for a while, seeing as they have Scandinavian roots (which they aren’t shy to boast on their posters, flags, and polaroids), and I’d heard good stories about Scandinavian burger chains in general.

Now I must say, there are many things to like about the place. The chill atmosphere, the clean interiors, the straightforward menu, the fast service, the fresh ingredients, and the honest approach. I must honestly say, though, I had my gripes, particularly with the burger…

Don’t get me wrong, it is a good burger in the altruistic sense. As I said, the ingredients are fresh, the bread is soft and well toasted, the meat is juicy and has a playful crunch, the overall concept of the burger is great, but it missed on two major points.

One, flavour. Past the zesty tang of the pickles (which i liked), the burger’s flavours were unfortunately mute. There was this subtle savoury undertone to the burger, but aside from that, there were no complimentary notes. No sweetness, no spice, no sharpness. I just wish there was more flavour to bring out these ingredients.

Second, the texture. Again, past the crunchy bits, it feels like biting through a softened block of cheese. The burger is extremely rich, to a fault even and could use some form of crisp to break the overwhelming creaminess of its body.

Overall, I do like the place, I see a lot of potential in it honestly, but until that potential is realised I must say you can find better burgers elsewhere.

The oldest coffee spot in Alexandria — King Farouk Coffee is a true gem.  absolutely unforgettable. A must-visit!

One of the most iconic cafes in Alexandria, Farouk cafe is part of the city’s heritage.

Established in 1928, the story behind its name is one of the nicest you’ll hear.

So one time when King Farouk was heading back to Ras El-Tin Palace, and among the crowds who were standing cheering and waving to their king, a blonde lady with blue eyes stood on the road in front of the king’s procession and was waving and calling for the king. Her name was MariePianotti

The guards tried to stop her and get her back in line, but she snuck between them and ran to the king’s car and saluted him with respect and asked him to have a drink at her cafe, which was called Kalimera Cafe.

The king agreed and went to the cafe and asked for hookah and tea, and as a sign of appreciation to the king who honored their cafe with his visit, she changed the name of the cafe to Farouk.

A popular restaurant where you can try the best kebdas in Alexandria. Frequented by Egyptians, the spiced liver sandwich is a real treat.

Kebda (or "kabda") is the Arabic word for liver, and it popularly refers to a very tasty Egyptian street food, especially Kebda Eskandarani (Alexandria style), which consists of tender beef liver sautéed with garlic, chili, cumin, and spices, commonly served in sandwiches with pita bread. It's a much-loved street food in Egypt, known for its strong and spicy flavor.

Each sandwich (it's not very big, and you can easily eat two or three) costs £15 (about 30 euro cents).

They serve it with lemon and a "piparra" (chili pepper) for the brave.

The atmosphere on the street (which is mostly pedestrianized) is very pleasant, and the waiters are super friendly.

A peaceful and pleasant seaside escape. It’s a gated neighborhood located directly next to the sea, designed for comfort and relaxation. The place is known for its wide range of furnished apartments and cabins available for short- or long-term rentals.

I stayed there for several days and it turned out to be one of the most comfortable and enjoyable experiences I've had in Alexandria. The accommodations are clean and well-maintained. The apartment we rented had modern furniture, proper kitchen tools, and a working air conditioner that made the stay much easier, especially during hot days. Everything inside was ready to use. It felt like a proper home, not just a rental unit.

What stood out most is the location. You can walk to the beach within minutes. The sea is very close, and the beach is clean and not too crowded. There are rental umbrellas and chairs, and it’s very family-friendly. It was easy to spend the whole day by the sea without needing to leave for anything.

Around the area, there are several small supermarkets, local bakeries, and many restaurants serving seafood, grills, and Egyptian dishes. You can also find juice bars and cafés. Everything you need is within walking distance. There’s no need for a car if you plan to stay inside the compound or nearby. It’s also very safe and secure.

What made the trip even more special was the atmosphere at night. Al-Ma’moura lights up with families, kids playing, music, and a lot of life. There are funfairs, bike rentals, small street performances, and open cafés where people gather to drink tea and chat. The vibe is relaxed and social. It’s easy to join the activities or simply enjoy the fresh sea breeze and night view.

The prices were affordable compared to other coastal areas. You get good value for the space, location, and access to everything nearby. Most of the rentals are family-owned, so there’s a personal touch in how they manage the units. You can even negotiate the price if you plan to stay longer. It’s a good option for both short weekend trips and longer summer holidays.

The compound is also suitable for kids. There are playgrounds and clean walking paths. For anyone looking for a simple, clean, and friendly environment by the sea, Al-Ma’moura delivers exactly that. It’s not a luxury resort, but it offers all the basics you need for a relaxing and enjoyable stay.

I would definitely return. The combination of clean housing, close beach access, and an active evening atmosphere made it a great choice. If you’re planning a trip to Alexandria and want to avoid crowded hotels, Al-Ma’moura Ashati is a solid, practical, and fun option.

Balbaa Restaurant in Sidi Beshr is one of those iconic Alexandria dining spots that immediately makes an impression. The place is lively, spacious, and full of energy, with the aroma of grills and spices filling the air as soon as you arrive. It has that classic Egyptian family-restaurant atmosphere, which adds to the overall experience.

The menu is extensive, especially if you’re a fan of grilled meats and traditional dishes. From kebabs and kofta to grilled chicken and liver, the selection is generous and offers something for everyone. The portions are big, and the presentation is straightforward but satisfying.

The food quality is generally good, with the grills being the highlight. The meats are tender and flavorful, though sometimes the seasoning can feel a bit strong depending on the dish. The restaurant really shines in its fresh salads and appetizers, which complement the grills perfectly.

Service is fast considering how busy the place usually gets, especially during peak hours or weekends. The staff are used to handling crowds and do their best to keep everything moving smoothly. Pricing is fair for the quantity and variety you get, though it can feel slightly high if you’re only ordering a few items.

Overall, Balbaa Restaurant in Sidi Beshr is definitely worth trying, especially if you enjoy Egyptian-style grills in a lively setting. It’s a great place for group meals or a hearty lunch, even if it may not be a spot you return to frequently. Still, it offers a solid and memorable dining experience in Alexandria.

My experience at Elbaraka Fried Chicken was genuinely very good and absolutely deserves a 5-star rating.

First of all, the food quality is excellent. The chicken is extremely tasty, well-seasoned, and cooked perfectly. Every bite was flavorful, crispy on the outside, and juicy on the inside. It’s clear that real attention is given to taste and consistency, which is not always easy to find. The flavors stand out and make the meal truly enjoyable.

One of the biggest positives is the portion size compared to the prices. The quantities are very generous, especially considering how reasonable the prices are. You really feel that you’re getting great value for your money, which makes the overall experience even more satisfying. It’s the kind of place where you leave full and happy without feeling that you overpaid.

Overall, it was a unique and memorable food experience, and definitely one that is worth repeating. If you’re looking for delicious fried chicken with great taste and generous portions, Elbaraka Fried Chicken is a strong choice.

That said, I do have one small observation. When we visited, the place was extremely crowded. While this is a clear sign of how popular and successful the restaurant is, it did affect the dine-in experience a bit. The seating area felt quite busy, and the chairs are not really designed for long or comfortable sitting. Because of that, the atmosphere wasn’t as relaxing as it could be, especially for those who prefer to sit and enjoy their meal comfortably.

However, this point does not take away from the excellent food quality and taste. As a food experience, Elbaraka Fried Chicken truly stands out, and I would happily return again—whether for a quick dine-in or takeaway.

Highly recommended for anyone who values great flavor, generous portions, and excellent value for money.

We have been in this station twice. The first time was complete chaos, we had a departure a 6pm and all the trains were behind schedule, there were hundreds if not thousands of people waiting in crowded spaces, people smoking, some yelling to be heard, trash everywhere, it was really bad. Second time we booked the latest train at 910pm, train came in at 930pm (not so bad) it was late at night so the station was almost deserted, a lot of people smoking still but we had room to move around and avoid them. So the second time, not as bad. When it comes to the trains, we booked first class the first time and second class (no room on first class) the second time, first class and second class (in comparison to trains in other countries) are more like second class and third class, but quite honestly not that bad. The seats are much more ample than planes (like first class airplane seats), they are very much apart from each other so you can recline further and be comfortable. The service people are fairly nice and everyone treated us with respect and were polite. The cabins were fairly clean and the coffee service is okay. They have air conditioner in first and second and they blast it, so, if you are traveling after sunset bring a blanket because you will get cold. Once out of the train station there's plenty of taxis and Uber, I personally use Uber in all of Egypt just because I have had bad experiences with taxi drivers changing their price mid-day, so I prefer to use Uber. Uber in Egypt is currently not accepting credit card payments so choose Cash and carry change with you to avoid any problems. Overall I love traveling by train so much more than traveling by plane, it is a so much easier in-and-out process than airports, if it takes 3 hours from Alexandria to Cairo by train and 45 minutes by plane but I have to arrive at the airport 2 hours prior to departure at the end it is almost the same amount of time, so I will continue using the Egyptian railways as much as I can even though I have to suffer a little at the stations. Word of advise, don't go to the bathrooms at the stations and be on time because if the trains are running on time there's a new train every 10 minutes or so, if you are late you will miss your train. Better be earlier than late.
